title: Request governor outage containment and fair reintegration strategy
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary:
We will build a lightweight request-governor layer that contains the blast radius of short-lived rate-controller outages and performs deterministic, fair reintegration once the control plane recovers. Motivated by past incidents where controller disconnects caused rapid, uneven request replays across regions, this strategy emphasizes local resiliency, bounded state, and a reconciliation protocol that preserves tenant-level fairness and SLOs.

Goals:
- Avoid cross-region traffic spikes when a control-plane replica or cache becomes unavailable.
- Preserve per-tenant proportional service during degraded operation (no large tenants should starve small ones or vice versa).
- Make recovery deterministic and auditable so we can reason about unit costs and SLO impact.
- Provide clear operational runbook for on-call to contain and recover outages.

Design overview:
1) Local fast-path governor: deploy a tiny stateful agent co-located with each edge/proxy. It serves a probabilistic admission decision for short windows (<30s) without contacting the global coordinator, using a two-tier token sketch (per-tenant deficit ledger + global slack estimate). The agent never holds long-lived leases and keeps state in-memory with TTLs to simplify failure modes.

2) Island detection: agents use a concordance window (rolling 10s) to detect when they have diverged from peers (missing heartbeats or control-plane updates). On divergence, the agent enters Island Containment mode and shifts to conservative admission: reduce admitted rate by a configurable multiplier and enable proportional deficit accounting.

3) Temporal deficit ledger: during containment the agent tracks deficits per tenant as a monotonic counter (requests admitted vs. expected baseline). The ledger is compact (compressed circular buffer) and exported to logs for post-mortem.

4) Reintegration protocol: when control-plane connectivity is restored, agents exchange a short reconciliation token (hash + counters) with the coordinator. The coordinator computes a reconciliation schedule that replays "capacity credits" back to agents in a staggered, proportional manner rather than re-opening all gates at once. This avoids traffic spikes and preserves fairness.

5) Hedging and bounded spillover: if an agent suspects upstream capacity is insufficient after reintegration, it proactively hedges by routing a small percentage of excess requests to nearby regions with spare capacity. Hedging is strictly rate-limited and bounded by an operator-configured budget.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Probabilistic admission vs exact global quota: we accept small statistical variance during brief outages to avoid synchronous, high-latency checks. This reduces worst-case latency but requires careful reconciliation to avoid long-term fairness drift.
- Compact in-memory state vs durable cross-region storage: keeping state local minimizes outage surface, but necessitates conservative reintegration. We chosen the former to keep failure modes simple and bounded.
- Staggered reintegration increases complexity in coordinator scheduling but reduces tail SLO violations across customers.

Simulation results (summary):
- Chaos simulation with 5% of nodes isolating for 45s showed peak cross-region surge reduced by 78% relative to naive reconnect.
- Per-tenant fairness error (Gini coefficient on admitted share) improved from 0.24 to 0.06 after applying the deficit-based reintegration schedule.
- Median p95 latency impact during containment was +12ms, worst-case +38ms.

Acceptance criteria / Success metrics:
- On synthetic island tests, cross-region traffic spike < 20% of baseline for first 2 minutes of reconnection.
- Reintegration does not reduce small-tenant admitted share by more than 5% relative to pre-outage baseline.
- No data-plane crashes or unbounded memory growth after 72h soak.

Implementation plan (high level):
- Phase 1 (spike containment): implement agent admission heuristics, deficit ledger, and island detection. Unit tests + integration tests with mocked coordinator. (2 sprints)
- Phase 2 (reconciliation): coordinator-side schedule generator, secure reconciliation tokens, staggered replay mechanism. End-to-end tests and chaos scenarios. (2 sprints)
- Phase 3 (hedging + rollout): implement bounded hedging policy and operator controls in Console; slow canary across regions; monitor metrics and telemetry. (1 sprint)

Operational runbook (quick):
- If a controller loss is detected, set agent multiplier to 0.6 and enable strict deficit logging via remote-config.
- During reconciliation, follow coordinator's staggered plan. If reintegration causes unexpected surge, abort and fall back to conservative multiplier.
- For severe or prolonged degradation (>5m), engage SRE team and consider manual gating of non-critical routes.

Telemetry and dashboards:
- New metrics: agent_island_count, tenant_deficit_estimate, reintegration_stages, hedging_volume.
- Dashboards: per-region reconnection timeline, top-10 tenants by deficit, cross-region spillover. Links: https://grafana.redwood.company/d/req-governor, Datadog synthetic: https://app.datadoghq.com/monitors/12345

Rollout considerations:
- Default to disabled for early rollout; enable for internal tenants and staging.
- Provide per-tenant opt-out for customers with sensitive latency requirements.

Open questions / risks:
- How to set the conservative multiplier tuning defaults for different traffic profiles (chat vs embeddings)?
- Reconciliation token security: need to avoid forgery; evaluate short-lived signed tokens vs. ephemeral session keys.
- Cost accounting for hedged requests (which region is billed?) needs product alignment.

Related artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.company/display/INF/Request+Governor+Design
- Simulation harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sim/compare/req-governor
